question: What is Rwanda's current legal and operating perimeter for virtual assets, payment service providers, e-money and a possible e-FRW; what did Law No. 023/2026 actually authorize and prohibit; what are the major banks actually doing; which claims and rails operate; and does the Ghana-Rwanda licence-passporting framework prove a cross-border payment or crypto route?
bluf: Rwanda now has an effective virtual-asset statute, but the reviewed official record does not yet show an operational licensing market. Law No. 023/2026 was gazetted and entered into force on 28 May 2026. It makes the Capital Market Authority the primary virtual-asset regulator, preserves a National Bank of Rwanda role over monetary stability and payments, requires licences or issuer approval, prohibits natural persons from carrying on virtual-asset business, treats virtual assets as non-legal-tender, and bars their direct use for payments unless NBR authorizes it. Stablecoins require prior CMA approval, full collateralization, liquid reserves, professional custody, audit and insolvency segregation; algorithmic stablecoins are excluded from the statutory virtual-asset category. Yet CMA's current regulation, application and licensee pages show no implementing virtual-asset regulation, VASP application route, VASP category, stablecoin issuer or approved virtual-asset product. The law is therefore effective while the public entry-and-authorization layer remains unproved. Rwanda's major banks remain conventional deposit, payment, securities-custody and cross-border-banking institutions: Bank of Kigali, BPR, I&M, Equity, Ecobank and Access disclose ordinary digital channels or regional transfers, but no reviewed primary source proves a Rwandan bank-issued stablecoin, tokenized deposit, crypto custody service, VASP licence or real-value token settlement. The e-FRW is still a proof of concept, and the Ghana-Rwanda passporting framework remains permission architecture rather than a transaction receipt.

authority.summary: Parliament owns statutes. Law No. 023/2026 makes CMA the virtual-asset Regulatory Authority, including licensing, issuer and product approval, inspection and rulemaking. NBR retains currency, payment-system, banking, e-money, PSP, financial-stability and CBDC authority and, under the new law, collaborates on monetary-stability, payment and systemic-risk matters and alone may approve direct virtual-asset payments. FIC owns financial-intelligence and AML/CFT/CPF functions; courts adjudicate offences and insolvency questions.
authority.boundary: Statute, implementing regulation, CMA licence, CMA issuer approval, NBR payment authorization, bank supervision, AML supervision and adjudication are different acts by different authorities.

legal_objects.summary: Law No. 023/2026 covers transferable or tradable digital value used for payment or investment, real-world tokenized assets and reserve-backed stable-value assets. It excludes digital fiat representations, NBR-regulated payment instruments, capital-market instruments, CBDC, closed-loop value, purely private non-trading value, NFTs, enhanced-anonymity assets and algorithmic stablecoins. The wider record separately preserves FRW cash, NBR settlement balances, bank deposits, e-money, safeguarded PSP funds, securities, covered virtual assets and a possible future e-FRW liability.
legal_objects.boundary: A statutory virtual asset, excluded algorithmic stablecoin, tokenized security, bank deposit, e-money claim, central-bank balance and CBDC are not interchangeable; exclusion from this law can mean another regime applies, not that the object is approved.

permitted_activities.summary: A CMA-licensed legal entity may provide the services enumerated in Article 14, including issuance/listing/trading platforms, clearing or settlement, fiat or virtual-asset exchange, transfer, order execution, placement, custody or administration, escrow, advice and investment management. Issuance, trading or listing of a virtual asset requires prior CMA approval; stablecoins have additional Article 19 duties. Natural persons may not conduct virtual-asset business. Virtual assets are not legal tender and may not be used directly to pay for goods, services, debts or financial obligations unless NBR authorizes that use. Mining facilities, crypto ATMs and mixers or tumblers require authorization.
permitted_activities.boundary: An activity named in effective law is not presently permitted to a person without the required licence or approval; statutory possibility, filed application, authorization, launch and first transaction remain separate.

entry_gates.summary: Article 10 requires a legal entity incorporated or registered in Rwanda with local presence, beneficial-owner disclosure, fit governance, regulatory capital and AML controls; regulations must prescribe procedures and capital. As of the cutoff, CMA's regulations page did not list a virtual-asset implementing regulation, its application page did not offer a VASP route, and its licensee page showed no VASP or approved issuer category. A June CMA procurement for virtual-asset consultancy indicates implementation work, not a licence window. Payment services still require the exact NBR licence, while Ghana passporting requires home permission, a Letter of No Objection and joint governance.
entry_gates.boundary: An effective framework law can coexist with an unproved implementing gateway; consultancy, awareness, application, home licence, no-objection letter, host permission, technical connection and first transaction are distinct clocks.

named_operating_actors.summary: NBR's supervised-bank list names nine commercial banks—Bank of Kigali, BPR Bank Rwanda, I&M Bank Rwanda, GT Bank, Ecobank Rwanda, Access Bank Rwanda, Equity Bank Rwanda, BOA Rwanda and NCBA Rwanda—plus BRD and ZIGAMA CSS. NBR says five unnamed D-SIBs held 75.6% of banking assets at December 2024, so this record does not invent a name-to-D-SIB mapping. Bank of Kigali, BPR, I&M, Equity, Ecobank and Access form the bank operating sample. CMA separately lists Bank of Kigali, BPR and I&M as traditional capital-market custodians, not virtual-asset custodians. The current CMA roster names no VASP, stablecoin issuer or approved virtual-asset product. NBR's November 2025 list names 42 conventional PSP entities; the Ghana-Rwanda pilot's four firms remain unnamed.
named_operating_actors.boundary: A bank, parent group, securities custodian, PSP, VASP, issuer and cross-border pilot participant are different legal and operating roles; a parent's activity elsewhere is not Rwandan-bank activity.

claims_and_backing.summary: Article 19 requires an approved stablecoin to be 100% collateralized at all times, bars lending reserve assets for yield, requires independent-auditor confirmation of liquidity for reasonable and timely redemption, verification means, a licensed professional custodian, regular audits and segregation from issuer and creditor assets for insolvency. Further regulations may still determine reserve-investment conditions. E-money remains a separately regulated redeemable issuer claim backed by at least equivalent authorized currency and safeguarded through trust or equivalent mechanisms; bank deposits remain bank liabilities subject to the DGF statute.
claims_and_backing.boundary: Statutory reserve design is not evidence that a stablecoin exists, that its assets were deposited, or that redemption worked; stablecoin reserves, e-money safeguarding, bank capital, deposit insurance and central-bank liability are separate protections.

domestic_rails.summary: NBR operates clearing and settlement facilities and modernised RIPPS; eKash supplies interoperable national P2P payments while mobile-money and bank PSPs supply customer interfaces. Current detailed RIPPS and eKash finality, exception and participant-default rulebooks were not retrieved.
domestic_rails.boundary: Customer display, PSP ledger, e-money transfer, eKash instruction, clearing and final NBR settlement are different records and clocks.

cross_border_routes.summary: The Ghana-Rwanda licence-passporting framework was signed in February 2025, approved in October 2025 and piloted with two PSPs from each country. It establishes a permission pathway but does not identify the firms, exact permissions or a completed payment. I&M's BRISK offers near-real-time USD, KES, TZS and UGX transfers among I&M entities and Ecobank markets conventional regional transfer products; neither is a crypto or token-settlement route. The e-FRW proof of concept only simulated cross-border flows and calls for a later live pilot with one partner central bank.
cross_border_routes.boundary: Mutual recognition, conventional correspondent or intragroup transfer, a Letter of No Objection, interoperability planning and simulated flow do not prove a cryptoasset, stablecoin or CBDC crossed a border; no crypto route arc is authorized.

operating_state.summary: Law No. 023/2026 is effective, but the public implementation layer remains incomplete or unproved: no virtual-asset regulation, application route, VASP licence, stablecoin issuer approval, bank token product or transaction appears in the reviewed CMA/NBR pages. The payment and e-money regimes, licensed PSPs, eKash and ordinary bank digital channels operate. Bank of Kigali's Open API concerns account checks, payments and bill settlement; BPR's and CMA's custody evidence concerns conventional securities; I&M and Ecobank cross-border products are fiat banking. The e-FRW remains a completed proof of concept rather than issued CBDC.
operating_state.boundary: Effective statute, implementing rule, open gateway, licensed actor, approved product, technical launch, first real-value transaction, recurring operation and issued CBDC are distinct states.

scale.summary: NBR reported 11 banks with FRW8.7 trillion of assets at December 2024 and five unnamed D-SIBs holding 75.6%. Bank-level public scale confirms a concentrated conventional system: Bank of Kigali reported Q1 2026 loans of FRW1.745 trillion and deposits of FRW1.895 trillion; BPR reported 2025 assets of FRW1.405 trillion and customer deposits of FRW874.0 billion; Ecobank reported 2025 assets of FRW636.9 billion and deposits of FRW552.2 billion. By June 2025, eKash had 20 onboarded institutions, 2.16 million active users and 25 million monthly transactions worth FRW105 billion. FIC identified nine commonly accessed VASPs, but no administrative VASP-license, stablecoin-reserve, bank-token, virtual-asset customer, balance or transaction series was found.
scale.boundary: Bank assets, deposits, PSP count and e-money traffic measure conventional finance; they are not crypto custody, tokenized deposits, stablecoin reserves or CBDC adoption.

stress.summary: FIC's assessment records high virtual-asset financial-crime risk and unregulated access. The new law requires reporting of fraud, theft, complaints and remedies, transaction tracing, cyber controls, continuity and freeze compliance, but no public administrative series yet demonstrates those controls in operation. Access Bank Rwanda's AML page classifies cryptocurrency dealers among prohibited businesses, a bank-specific risk policy rather than national law. NBR reports D-SIB resolvability assessments and a crisis simulation for banks; the CBDC proof of concept identifies privacy, cyber, device, failed-transaction and lost-credential risks. No primary-source national virtual-asset failure, custody shortfall, bank-token incident, loss or recovery series was located.
stress.boundary: Risk assessment, bank client policy, statutory control, supervisory exercise, observed incident, quantified loss, judgment and distribution are separate evidence states.

correction_and_loss.summary: The virtual-asset law allows a competent authority to order freezes for substantiated suspected illegality, sanctions or investigations; requires VASPs to safeguard customer assets, preserve originator and beneficiary records, screen addresses and report fraud, theft, complaints and remediation; and places unauthorized business, issuance, marketing, payments, mining facilities, ATMs and mixers under criminal penalties. Stablecoin reserves must be insolvency-segregated. Separately, payment-law safeguards, bank-resolution powers and the DGF protect different conventional claims. No reviewed evidence shows a licensed VASP insolvency, stablecoin redemption, customer-asset distribution or freeze-and-recovery case under the new law.
correction_and_loss.boundary: Address freeze, balance reduction, ledger correction, refund, safeguarded-fund claim, stablecoin reserve claim, bank resolution, deposit-guarantee payout and criminal restitution have different owners and clocks.

evidence_boundary.summary: This recertification uses the Official Gazette law, live CMA regulation/application/licensee pages, NBR system and bank records, exact bank disclosures, FIC, Bank of Ghana and the Rwanda governor. It treats the absence of a public implementation object as a bounded negative result, not proof that CMA received no private inquiry. It does not convert CMA's conventional securities-custodian category, ordinary bank APIs or fiat regional transfers into crypto custody or token settlement, and does not attribute foreign-parent activity to a Rwandan subsidiary.
evidence_boundary.boundary: Fresh research is not Chronicle promotion, investment advice, publication authority, app shipment, proof of a licence, or proof of a crypto corridor.
